summary: This note outlines the history of New Zealand, from its settlement by Polynesians at least 700 years ago through European contact. It covers Abel Tasman's 1642 sighting, James Cook's mapping voyages, and the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi that brought New Zealand into the British Empire. It ends by noting the later shift of most land from Māori to Pākehā ownership.
one_line: Overview of New Zealand's history from Polynesian settlement and Abel Tasman's 1642 sighting through Cook's voyages and the 1840 Treaty of Waitangi.
key_facts: New Zealand was discovered and settled by Polynesians at least 700 years ago, who developed a distinct Māori culture centred on kinship links and land.
Dutch navigator Abel Tasman was the first European explorer to sight New Zealand, on 13 December 1642.
The Dutch were the first non-natives to explore and chart New Zealand's coastline.
Captain James Cook reached New Zealand in October 1769 on the first of his three voyages and was the first European explorer to circumnavigate and map it.
Tasman anchored in Golden Bay at the northern end of the South Island in December 1642 and named it Murderers' Bay.
Tasman called the land Staten Landt, after the States General of the Netherlands, and that name appeared on his first maps of the country.
In 1645 Dutch cartographers changed the name to Nova Zeelandia in Latin, from Nieuw Zeeland, after the Dutch province of Zeeland.
James Cook of HM Bark Endeavour anglicised the name as New Zealand; he visited the islands during 1769 to 1770.
The Treaty of Waitangi was signed in 1840 between the British Crown and various Māori chiefs, bringing New Zealand into the British Empire.
The Treaty of Waitangi gave Māori the same rights as British subjects.
On 6 February 1840, Hobson and about forty Māori chiefs signed the Treaty of Waitangi at Waitangi in the Bay of Islands.
In total, more than five hundred Māori eventually signed the Treaty of Waitangi after copies were taken around the country.
Extensive British settlement occurred through the rest of the 19th century and into the early 20th century.
War and a European economic and legal system led to most of New Zealand's land passing from Māori to Pākehā ownership, leaving most Māori impoverished.
